claim: Cryo-EM structures of the myosin VI motor domain bound to F-actin were obtained at 4.6 Å resolution in the rigor state and 5.5 Å resolution in the Mg-ADP state.
source: Here we present cryo-EM reconstructions of myosin VI bound to F-actin in the rigor state at 4.6 Å resolution and the ADP state at 5.5 Å resolution along with corresponding atomistic models.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the resolutions achieved for both reconstructions in the abstract and results sections, with supporting FSC curves in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: There is an almost complete lack of conservation of residues at the actin-myosin interface between myosin VI and myosin IIC despite preservation of the primary sequence regions composing it.
source: Comparison to the myosin IIC-F-actin rigor complex reveals an almost complete lack of conservation of residues at the actin-myosin interface despite preservation of the primary sequence regions composing it, suggesting an evolutionary path for motor specialization.
evidence: The claim is supported by detailed structural comparisons shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, demonstrating different specific interactions at conserved interface regions.

claim: The transition from ADP to rigor provides a structural rationale for force sensitivity in this step of the mechanochemical cycle.
source: Additionally, analysis of the transition from ADP to rigor provides a structural rationale for force sensitivity in this step of the mechanochemical cycle.
evidence: The manuscript presents structural data showing lever arm bending and converter rearrangements between ADP and rigor states (Figure 5), which are proposed to be mechanically regulated.

claim: Reciprocal rearrangements in actin and myosin accompany the transition between ADP and rigor states.
source: Finally, we observe reciprocal rearrangements in actin and myosin accompanying the transition between these states, supporting a role for actin structural plasticity during force generation by myosin VI.
evidence: Figure 6 shows conformational changes in both the actin D-loop and H-plug regions accompanying myosin state transitions.

claim: Myosin VI is unique in its ability to walk 'backwards' towards actin filament pointed ends.
source: In this study, we focus on the MD of myosin VI, an unconventional myosin motor unique in its ability to walk 'backwards' towards actin filament pointed ends (Wells et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a well-established property of myosin VI supported by citation to Wells et al., 1999.

claim: The large insert two in the myosin VI lever arm confers reverse directionality to the motor.
source: The large insert two in the myosin VI lever arm confers reverse directionality to the motor (Bryant et al., 2007; Park et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bryant et al., 2007 and Park et al., 2007.

claim: The myosin VI converter region adopts a unique conformation contributing to the large motor step size.
source: and the adjacent converter region adopts a unique conformation contributing to the large motor step size (Ménétrey et al., 2007; Ovchinnikov et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Myosin VI functions in endocytosis, intracellular transport, and stereocilia maintenance.
source: Myosin VI functions in endocytosis (Altman et al., 2007; Buss et al., 2001; Morris et al., 2002), intracellular transport (Inoue et al., 2008), and stereocilia maintenance (Avraham et al., 1995; Hertzano et al., 2008; Melchionda et al., 2001; Seiler et al., 2004)
evidence: Multiple citations support these functional roles.

claim: Myosin VI has been implicated in deafness and cancers.
source: and it has been implicated in deafness (Ahmed et al., 2003; Melchionda et al., 2001; Mohiddin et al., 2004) and cancers (Dunn et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2016; Yoshida et al., 2004).
evidence: Citations to multiple studies support these disease associations.

claim: The switch II loop (swII) adopts an open conformation in the phosphate release (PiR) state, opening a path for phosphate escape.
source: The PiR structure revealed that swII adopts an open conformation in this state, opening a path that would allow phosphate escape from the nucleotide binding pocket (Llinas et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on a previous crystal structure study cited.

claim: In both the ADP and rigor states, switch II adopts a closed conformation.
source: Consistent with this model, we find that in both the ADP and rigor states, as with the PPS and post-rigor state structures, swII adopts a closed conformation when compared to the PiR state (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Figure 4B and C show the closed conformation of swII in both states compared to the open PiR state.

claim: The major converter rearrangement occurs from PiR to ADP, with the converter adopting a post-power stroke, rigor-like conformation in the ADP state.
source: By comparing all previously crystalized converter conformations with our density maps (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), we confirm that the major converter rearrangement occurs from PiR to ADP, with the converter adopting a post-power stroke, rigor-like conformation in this state (Figure 4D).
evidence: Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 show the converter conformations and their fits to density maps.

claim: A ~30° rotation of the converter around an axis nearly parallel to the actin filament accompanies the transition from ADP to rigor.
source: We observe a ~ 30° rotation of the converter around an axis nearly parallel to the actin filament upon the transition from ADP to rigor (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Video 3).
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Video 3 demonstrate this rotation.

claim: The rigor lever arm displays a prominent bend between insert 2 residues 784 and 785, which is absent in the ADP state.
source: As was observed in the rigor-like crystal structure (Ménétrey et al., 2005), the rigor lever arm displays a prominent bend between insert 2 residues 784 and 785, which our map and model reveals to be absent in the ADP state (Figure 5C and D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 5C and D show the bent lever arm in rigor and straight lever arm in ADP.

claim: The converter rotation and lever arm bending results in a ~35 Å displacement of the tip of the modeled lever arm, with a ~10 Å projected displacement along the filament axis towards the pointed end.
source: The converter rotation and lever arm bending results in a ~ 35 Å displacement of the tip of our modeled lever arm, with a ~ 10 Å projected displacement along the filament axis towards the pointed end (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is calculated from the structural models shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The actin protomer adopts a unique conformation in each of the three states (actin alone, ADP-bound, and rigor), with local deformations occurring at the actomyosin interface and at distal lateral contacts in the interior of the filament.
source: Despite this preservation of filament architecture, the actin protomer adopts a unique conformation in each of the three states, with local deformations occurring at the actomyosin interface mediated by the D loop and, intriguingly, at distal lateral contacts in the interior of the filament mediating the interaction between the two strands of the actin filament (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Videos 6 and 7).
evidence: Figure 6 shows the conformational changes in actin across the three states.

claim: The refined helical parameters are essentially identical for all three filament states (actin alone, ADP-bound, and rigor).
source: The refined helical parameters are essentially identical for all three filament states we report here (Table 1), in contrast to both myosin IIC and myosin V, where myosin binding has been reported to induce a 0.5–0.8° change in azimuthal rotation (von der Ecken et al., 2016; Wulf et al., 2016).
evidence: Table 1 shows the helical parameters (rise and twist) are nearly identical across states.

claim: R39 in the actin D-loop forms a direct contact with E270 in the H-plug across the lateral interface between actin strands.
source: Although the D-loop and H-plug are distal from one another within a single subunit, they are brought into close proximity between laterally adjacent protomers within the filament, and a single side-chain pair, D-loop residue R39 and H-plug residue E270, makes a direct contact between them across the interface (Figure 6E).
evidence: Figure 6E shows the R39-E270 interaction across the actin strands.

claim: R39 additionally forms a canonical head-to-head salt-bridge interaction with D286 of subdomain 3 of a longitudinally adjacent subunit.
source: R39 additionally forms a canonical head-to-head salt-bridge interaction with D286 of subdomain 3 of a longitudinally adjacent subunit, placing this residue at a vertex that connects three actin subunits along and across the strands of the filament (Figure 6E).
evidence: Figure 6E shows the R39-D286 salt bridge interaction.

claim: The actomyosin interface is comprised of several myosin surface loops (HCM loop, loop 2, loop 3, loop 4, and helix-loop-helix) located within the upper 50 KD (U50) and lower 50 KD (L50) domains of myosin which interact with subdomains 1 and 3 of one actin, and subdomain 2 of an adjacent actin.
source: As with myosin IIC, the actomyosin interface is comprised of several myosin surface loops (HCM loop, loop 2, loop 3, loop 4, and helix-loop-helix) located within the upper 50 KD (U50) and lower 50 KD (L50) domains of myosin which interact with subdomains 1 and 3 of one actin, and subdomain 2 of an adjacent actin (Figure 2A), supporting overall conservation of the interface architecture (Behrmann et al., 2012; Holmes et al., 2003; Rayment et al., 1993; Várkuti et al., 2012; von der Ecken et al., 2016).
evidence: Figure 2A shows the overall architecture of the actomyosin interface with labeled regions.

claim: In myosin VI, the hydrophobic residues P536 and L535 of the HLH are embedded in a groove comprised of I345, L349, and Y143 in actin SD1.
source: In myosin VI we find that the hydrophobic residues P536 and L535 of the HLH are embedded in a groove comprised of I345, L349, and Y143 in actin SD1 (Figure 2B), with clear density peaks to support positioning of these side chains.
evidence: Figure 2B shows the HLH-actin hydrophobic interaction with density map support.

claim: For myosin IIC, the HLH is comprised of aromatic side chains, with F560 playing a critical role in the interaction with actin.
source: However, the other specific residues involved in the interaction differ substantially (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B). In contrast to myosin VI, the myosin IIC HLH is comprised of aromatic side chains, with F560 playing a critical role in the interaction with actin (von der Ecken et al., 2016).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1B shows the myosin IIC HLH interface, and the claim is supported by citation to von der Ecken et al., 2016.

claim: The large loop 3 of myosin VI likely makes more extensive contacts at the Milligan contact interface than myosin IIC.
source: However, the size of loop three varies among myosins, which prior studies have suggested may relate to its prominence in the actomyosin interface (Van Dijk et al., 1999). Consistent with this prediction, the large loop 3 of myosin VI likely makes more extensive contacts at this interface than myosin IIC, with MDFF suggesting probable interactions formed between D574 in loop three and K50 in the actin D loop, and E575 and R95 in actin SD2 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Figure 2C shows the loop 3 interactions, and the claim is supported by citation to Van Dijk et al., 1999.

claim: The E575 residue in myosin VI loop 3 is not conserved among any other myosin isoforms.
source: The E575 residue is not conserved among any other myosin isoforms, suggesting that this interaction may be specific to myosin VI (Zhang and Liao, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang and Liao, 2012.

claim: Myosin VI R561 forms a cation-π interaction with Y91 in actin.
source: An additional unanticipated contact is made by myosin VI R561, which forms a cation-π interaction with Y91 in actin in our model (Figure 3C), discussed further in the next section.
evidence: Figure 3C shows the R561-Y91 cation-π interaction in the rigor state.

claim: E354 in loop 4 of the U50 domain of myosin VI likely forms a salt bridge with K328 in actin SD3.
source: In addition to the Milligan contact interactions, MDFF suggests myosin VI makes another unique electrostatic interaction with F-actin. E354 in loop 4 (A355-C362) of the U50 domain of myosin likely forms a salt bridge with K328 in actin SD3 (Figure 2D) as supported by clear density for side chains in this region.
evidence: Figure 2D shows the E354-K328 interaction with density support.

claim: The myosin VI HCM loop base likely forms an electrostatic interaction with actin, with a potential salt bridge between R393 and E334 of actin SD1.
source: In contrast with myosin IIC, the ordered myosin VI HCM base likely forms an electrostatic interaction with actin, as MDFF suggests a potential salt bridge between R393 and E334 of actin SD1 (Figure 2F).
evidence: Figure 2F shows the R393-E334 interaction.

claim: Very few changes in the actin binding cleft are observed between the ADP and rigor state atomistic models.
source: We find very few changes in the actin binding cleft between the ADP and rigor state atomistic models, which are predominantly subtle local rearrangements which do not impact overall cleft closure (Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Figure 3A and B show minimal cleft rearrangements between ADP and rigor states.

claim: The Cα RMSD between the U50 and L50 from the rigor and ADP states are 1.5 Å and 1.1 Å, respectively.
source: The Cα RMSD between the U50 and L50 from the rigor and ADP states are 1.5 Å and 1.1 Å, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the structural models.

claim: Centroid distances of the U50 and L50 between the ADP and rigor states are 0.6 Å and 0.5 Å.
source: Additionally, centroid distances of the U50 and L50 between the two states are 0.6 Å and 0.5 Å, demonstrating that there is minimal cleft movement (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The cation-π interaction between R561 in loop three with Y91 of actin SD2 is not present in the ADP state but forms upon the transition to rigor.
source: Analysis of side chain interactions suggested by MDFF shows that nearly all interactions are likely to be maintained between the two states (Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4), with the exception of a single residue pair at the Milligan contact. The cation-π interaction between R561 in loop three with Y91 of actin SD2 is not present for the ADP state, suggesting that this contact is likely to form upon the transition from ADP to rigor (Figure 3C).
evidence: Figure 3C shows the absence of this interaction in ADP and its presence in rigor.

claim: Density for R561 is present in the rigor state reconstruction, but notably absent in the ADP state, consistent with R561 being disordered in the ADP state.
source: Supporting this model, density for R561 is present in the rigor state reconstruction, but notably absent in the ADP state, consistent with R561 being disordered in this state (Figure 3C).
evidence: Figure 3C shows the presence/absence of density for R561 in the two states.

claim: R561 is conserved with only one other human myosin.
source: Previous sequence analysis suggests R561 is conserved with only one other human myosin (Zhang and Liao, 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang and Liao, 2012.

claim: A similar R561-Y91 cation-π interaction is absent in both myosin IIC and myosin V structures.
source: and a similar interaction is absent in both myosin IIC and myosin V structures (Figure 3—figure supplement 6), suggesting that this interaction may have evolved to support the specialized properties of myosin VI.
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 6 shows the absence of this interaction in myosin IIC and V.

claim: The transducer adopts a strained conformation in the ADP state, which is relieved upon nucleotide release in myosin VI.
source: As actin binding cleft changes are minimal, alternative mechanisms may also be involved in increasing the affinity of the rigor state. In myosin V, the transducer, a large β-sheet linking the nucleotide-binding cleft to the actin-binding cleft, was reported to adopt a strained conformation in the ADP state, which is relieved upon nucleotide release (Wulf et al., 2016). This motivated a model in which an effective increase in actin binding affinity resulted from relief of intramolecular strain in the MD as opposed to a conformational change which modifies contacts with actin. We observe a similar rearrangement of the transducer in myosin VI (Figure 3—figure supplement 5)
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 5 shows transducer rearrangements, and the claim is supported by citation to Wulf et al., 2016.

claim: Comparison of the HR MDFF rigor model to the crystal structure of myosin VI in rigor-like state in the absence of actin (2BKI) demonstrates increased jaw closure to relieve a clash with the filament.
source: Comparison of the HR MDFF rigor model to the crystal structure of myosin VI in rigor-like state in the absence of actin (2BKI) demonstrates increased jaw closure to relieve a clash with the filament (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), highlighting the importance of visualizing the motor bound to actin to determine the structure of the rigor state.
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1F shows the jaw closure comparison.

claim: Combining datasets with and without RNA bound improved the resolution of the reconstruction considerably, suggesting that RNA binding does not alter motor conformation.
source: Combining datasets with and without RNA bound improved the resolution of our reconstruction considerably, suggesting that RNA binding does not alter motor conformation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1B shows FSC curves demonstrating improved resolution when datasets are combined.

claim: The level of detail in the cryo-EM map decays radially outward from the center of the filament.
source: As is often the case with helically symmetric specimens, the level of detail in the map decays radially outward from the center of the filament (Kucukelbir et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a known characteristic of helical reconstructions, supported by citation to Kucukelbir et al., 2014.

claim: Local resolution analysis suggests a gradient from slightly better than 4 Å in the actin region to around 6 Å resolution in the converter and lever arm.
source: Local resolution analysis suggests a gradient from slightly better than 4 Å in the actin region of the map, where large side-chains are definitively resolved, to around 6 Å resolution in the converter and lever arm, where only the contour of the backbone is visible (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E shows the local resolution analysis.

claim: No density was present for two regions of the MD, loop two and the Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM) loop, consistent with flexibility.
source: No density was present for two regions of the MD, loop two and the Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM) loop, consistent with flexibility, and only the molecular dynamics force field influenced their conformation (Figure 1C, red).
evidence: Figure 1C shows the regions where density was absent.

claim: The HR MDFF rigor model converged well with a molprobity score of 1.44 and a clash score of 0.41.
source: The resulting atomistic model ('HR', high-resolution) converged well with a molprobity score of 1.44 and a clash score of 0.41 (Table 1).
evidence: Table 1 shows the validation statistics for the model.

claim: The HR ADP MDFF model converged well with a molprobity score of 1.40 and a clash score of 0.33.
source: The resulting atomistic model (HR) converged well with a molprobity score of 1.40 and a clash score of 0.33 (Table 1).
evidence: Table 1 shows the validation statistics for the ADP model.

claim: The challenge of obtaining high-quality micrographs of the lower-affinity ADP-bound state limited the number of segments incorporated into the ADP reconstruction.
source: The challenge of obtaining high-quality micrographs of this lower-affinity actin-bound state limited the number of segments incorporated into this reconstruction.
evidence: This is stated as a technical limitation affecting the ADP state reconstruction.

claim: A clear density peak is observed in the nucleotide-binding cleft in the ADP state that is absent from the rigor density map, as expected for bound ADP.
source: We observe a clear density peak in the cleft (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) that is absent from the rigor density map, as expected for bound ADP; however, the limited resolution precludes detailed modelling of the nucleotide.
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1 shows the density for ADP in the nucleotide-binding pocket.

claim: MDFF models of the ADP state more closely resemble each other than the rigor state, regardless of the starting model used.
source: Regardless of the starting model, MDFF models of the ADP state more closely resemble each other than the rigor state, suggesting our fitting procedure is capturing structural differences between these states that are represented in the maps.
evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Table 2 show RMSD comparisons between different models.

claim: Myosin VI affinity for actin increases as it progresses through the force generation cycle, with the rigor state exhibiting approximately 10-fold higher affinity for actin than the ADP state.
source: Myosin VI affinity for actin increases as it progresses through the force generation cycle, with the rigor state exhibiting approximately 10-fold higher affinity for actin than the ADP state (De La Cruz et al., 2001; Robblee et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to De La Cruz et al., 2001 and Robblee et al., 2004.

claim: Pyrene quenching data indicated that cleft closure occurs immediately after Pi release.
source: While pyrene quenching data (Llinas et al., 2015) indicated that cleft closure occurs immediately after Pi release
evidence: This is supported by citation to Llinas et al., 2015.

claim: The major structural changes leading to actin-binding cleft closure must precede the ADP state.
source: Atomistic models derived from intermediate-resolution cryo-EM reconstructions for myosin V bound to F-actin also showed minimal cleft rearrangements between the ADP and rigor states (Wulf et al., 2016), in agreement with our findings that the major structural changes leading to actin-binding cleft closure must precede the ADP state.
evidence: This is supported by the minimal cleft changes observed between ADP and rigor, and citation to Wulf et al., 2016.

claim: Formation of the R561-Y91 cation-π contact could play a role in increasing affinity for actin in the ADP to rigor transition of myosin VI.
source: Formation of this contact could play a role in increasing affinity for actin in the ADP to rigor transition of myosin VI; future high-resolution structural studies will be required to establish if analogous minor adjustments to the filament binding interface play a role in myosin V, as well as other myosins during this transition.
evidence: This is proposed based on the observation that this interaction forms upon transition from ADP to rigor.

claim: The major power stroke is accomplished by a converter rearrangement licensed by cleft closure immediately upon phosphate release.
source: Our structural data are thus consistent with a model in which the major power stroke is accomplished by a converter rearrangement licensed by cleft closure immediately upon phosphate release (Figure 4E) (Llinas et al., 2015).
evidence: Figure 4E shows the schematic of this transition, and the claim is supported by citation to Llinas et al., 2015.

claim: The converter rotation is sterically coupled to nucleotide cleft opening by opposing motions in the SH1 helix and the long relay helix.
source: This repositioning is sterically coupled to nucleotide cleft opening by opposing motions in the SH1 helix, which transitions from an extended to compact conformation, and the long relay helix, which exhibits winding at the end proximal to the converter (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, and Video 4).
evidence: Figure 5A, B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2 show the SH1 and relay helix rearrangements.

claim: The relay helix contacts the transducer, which coordinates movement of the switch I and N-terminal loops away from the nucleotide-binding pocket.
source: The relay helix contacts the transducer, which coordinates movement of the switch I (residues 193–205) and N-terminal loops (residues 96–106 and 305–312) away from the nucleotide-binding pocket (Figure 5A, Video 2, and Video 5).
evidence: Figure 5A and Videos 2 and 5 show these coordinated movements.

claim: The SH1 helix is connected to the cleft loop (residues 670–681), which displays coherent displacement away from the cleft in the opposite direction.
source: The SH1 helix is connected to an unnamed loop we here refer to as the cleft loop (residues 670–681), which unexpectedly displays coherent displacement away from the cleft in the opposite direction (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Figure 5A and B show the cleft loop displacement.

claim: Bending of the lever arm produces a 30° reorientation, with the lever arm protruding off the filament axis in the ADP state but almost perfectly parallel to the filament in the rigor state.
source: Based on these grafted models, bending produces a 30° reorientation of the lever arm, which protrudes off the filament axis in the ADP state but is almost perfectly parallel to the filament in the rigor state, providing a new explanation for early EM observations (Wells et al., 1999).
evidence: Figure 5C and D show the lever arm bending, and the claim is supported by citation to Wells et al., 1999.

claim: A bent lever arm and the interaction between E14 in the proximal light chain and K736/R732 are sterically incompatible with the ADP converter position.
source: A bent lever arm and this interaction are sterically incompatible with the ADP converter position, which would cause severe clashes between the proximal light chain and the MD (Figure 5E).
evidence: Figure 5E shows the steric clash that would occur.

claim: Nucleotide release is coupled to a converter rotation that licenses a lever arm bend in myosin VI.
source: Our models suggest that nucleotide release is coupled to a converter rotation that licenses a lever arm bend in myosin VI, contributing to the displacement observed in previous structural and functional studies of the ADP to rigor transition (Lister et al., 2004; Wells et al., 1999) (Figure 5F).
evidence: Figure 5F shows the schematic of this mechanism, supported by citations to Lister et al., 2004 and Wells et al., 1999.

claim: The mechanism of lever arm bending coupled to ADP release is not responsible for the small lever arm swing reported in myosin V, which lacks insert 2.
source: This mechanism is clearly not responsible for the small lever arm swing recently reported to be coupled to ADP release in myosin V, which lacks insert 2 (Wulf et al., 2016); rather, it provides a distinct, additional mechanism for myosin VI to reposition the lever arm between the ADP and rigor states.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wulf et al., 2016 and the structural difference (presence/absence of insert 2).

claim: Force could gate nucleotide engagement by regulating lever arm bending and the associated converter repositioning.
source: Furthermore, we propose that force could gate nucleotide engagement by regulating lever arm bending and the associated converter repositioning, with differential effects depending on the geometry (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the structural observations.

claim: The lower resolution of the actin-alone reconstruction vs. those bound to myosin suggests that myosin binding may rigidify the filament and reduce inherent conformational flexibility.
source: The lower resolution of this reconstruction vs. those bound to myosin suggests that myosin binding may rigidify the filament and reduce inherent conformational flexibility (Galkin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the resolution differences and supported by citation to Galkin et al., 2012.

claim: The D-loop is a flexible region of actin SD2 that can adopt a range of conformations to facilitate longitudinal contacts during actin polymerization.
source: The D-loop is a flexible region of actin SD2 that can adopt a range of conformations to facilitate longitudinal contacts during actin polymerization (Dominguez and Holmes, 2011; Galkin et al., 2010; Otterbein et al., 2001) and engage with actin binding partners (Dominguez and Holmes, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies on actin structure.

claim: The D-loop shifts upon myosin VI binding, orienting slightly towards the MD, consistent with what has been reported for myosin IIC and IE.
source: Consistent with what has previously been reported for myosin IIC (von der Ecken et al., 2016) and IE (Behrmann et al., 2012), this flexible loop also shifts upon myosin VI binding, orienting slightly towards the MD (Figure 6B–C and Video 3).
evidence: Figure 6B-C shows the D-loop shift, and the claim is supported by citations to von der Ecken et al., 2016 and Behrmann et al., 2012.

claim: Both the ADP and rigor states exhibit excursions of the D-loop relative to the unbound state, with a Cα RMSD of 1.0 Å in both cases.
source: Both the ADP and rigor states exhibit excursions of the D-loop relative to the unbound state, with a Cα RMSD of 1.0 Å in both cases (Figure 6D).
evidence: Figure 6D shows the RMSD quantification.

claim: The Cα RMSD of the D-loop between the ADP and rigor states is 0.9 Å, demonstrating that the D-loop adopts distinct conformational states as the myosin force generation cycle proceeds.
source: The Cα RMSD between the ADP and rigor states is also of a similar magnitude (0.9 Å, Figure 6D), demonstrating that the D-loop adopts distinct conformational states as the myosin force generation cycle proceeds.
evidence: Figure 6D shows the RMSD quantification.

claim: The hydrophobic plug (H-plug, residues 263–273) adjoins three actin subunits within the filament lattice, fitting into the groove created by the interface between two actin subunits on the adjacent filament strand.
source: The historically named hydrophobic plug (H-plug, residues 263–273) adjoins three actin subunits within the filament lattice, fitting into the groove created by the interface between two actin subunits on the adjacent filament strand (Chen et al., 1993; Holmes et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 1993 and Holmes et al., 1990.

claim: The R39-E270 interaction acts as an allosteric relay, where myosin remodeling of the D-loop necessitates repositioning of the H-plug due to steric exclusion.
source: We propose that this bi-partite interaction acts as an allosteric relay. As myosin VI remodels its binding site on actin, primarily through rearrangements of the D-loop, movement of the R39-D286 bridge necessitates repositioning of E270 due to steric exclusion. However, the electrostatic attraction between E270 and R39 prevents rotameric exchange of E270, producing instead a distortion of the H-plug.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the structural observations.

claim: The actomyosin interface is a highly evolvable interaction surface despite fundamental conservation of enzymatic mechanism across the myosin superfamily.
source: Despite the fundamental conservation of enzymatic mechanism across the myosin superfamily, our studies unambiguously demonstrate that the actomyosin interface is a highly evolvable interaction surface.
evidence: This is concluded from the comparison of myosin VI and IIC interfaces showing divergent residues.

claim: Comparing myosin IIC and myosin VI, only a single identical actin-binding residue is observed: myosin IIC P561/myosin VI P536 in the HLH.
source: Comparing myosin IIC and myosin VI, we observe only a single identical actin-binding residue, myosin IIC P561/myosin VI P536 in the HLH; all other interfacial residues have diverged despite the high degree of conservation of the nucleotide-binding pocket (Figure 7A).
evidence: Figure 7A shows the conservation analysis.

claim: The myosin VI interface residues identified are essentially completely conserved between species.
source: The myosin VI interface residues we have identified are essentially completely conserved between species (Figure 7A), and likely contribute to this motor's specialization.
evidence: Figure 7A shows the conservation analysis across 47 organisms.

claim: Rearward force applied to the lead head would disfavor the lever arm bend and thus promote the ADP-bound state.
source: Lever arm bending is coupled to converter rearrangements, which, through the SH1 and relay helices, promotes nucleotide cleft opening and ADP release (Figures 5A, B and 7B). Rearward force applied to the lead head would disfavor the lever arm bend and thus promote the ADP-bound state; conversely, forward load would promote bending and thus favor the rigor state (Figure 7B).
evidence: Figure 7B shows the schematic of force effects on the ADP-rigor transition.

claim: Forward load would promote lever arm bending and thus favor the rigor state.
source: conversely, forward load would promote bending and thus favor the rigor state (Figure 7B).
evidence: Figure 7B shows the schematic of force effects.

claim: Extreme rearward force locks the motor in the ADP state, facilitating a transition from processive transporter to actin-bound tether.
source: This framework is consistent with a model wherein extreme rearward force locks the motor in the ADP state, facilitating a transition from processive transporter to actin-bound tether (Altman et al., 2004; Chuan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Altman et al., 2004 and Chuan et al., 2011.

claim: The proposed force-sensitivity mechanism agrees with biochemical data demonstrating an increase in ADP dissociation rate under forward load and increased affinity for ADP under rearward load.
source: This proposal agrees with biochemical data demonstrating an increase in ADP dissociation rate under forward load and increased affinity for ADP under rearward load (Altman et al., 2004; Oguchi et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Altman et al., 2004 and Oguchi et al., 2008.

claim: The proposed force-sensitivity mechanism is consistent with recent simulation studies suggesting the converter can adopt a post-powerstroke conformation in the presence of force.
source: and it is also consistent with recent simulation studies suggesting the converter can adopt a post-powerstroke conformation in the presence of force (Mugnai and Thirumalai, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mugnai and Thirumalai, 2017.

claim: Strain energy may be stored in the actin filament as the force generation cycle proceeds, with the filament being maximally strained when the motor is most stably bound in rigor.
source: As we observe the conformation of the H-plug becomes increasingly deformed as the motor proceeds from ADP to rigor, with increasing RMSD relative to the ground-state of unbound actin (Figure 6D), we speculate that this segment is adopting an increasingly unfavorable conformation as the binding affinity of the actomyosin interface increases, suggesting strain energy may be stored in the filament as the force generation cycle proceeds (Figure 7A).
evidence: Figure 6D shows the increasing RMSD, and Figure 7A shows the schematic.

claim: The D-loop acts as a 'handle' which enables myosin VI to transmit conformational changes from the filament surface through an allosteric relay to the H-plug.
source: We propose that the D-loop acts as a 'handle' which enables myosin VI, and potentially other actin-binding proteins, to transmit conformational changes from the filament surface through an allosteric relay to the H-plug (Figure 7A), converting binding energy into strain energy.
evidence: Figure 7A shows the schematic of this mechanism.

claim: Strain energy stored in the filament may facilitate MD displacement as ATP rebinds during the transition to post-rigor, with elastic recoil in the actin filament helping to drive this transition forward.
source: As our data suggest that the filament is maximally strained when the motor is most stably bound in rigor, one possibility we envision is that strain energy stored in the filament facilitates MD displacement as ATP rebinds during the transition to post-rigor, with elastic recoil in the actin filament helping to drive this transition forward (Figure 7A).
evidence: Figure 7A shows the schematic of this proposed mechanism.

claim: D-loop remodeling by myosin IIC does not produce H-plug distortion.
source: Examination of the actomyosin IIC rigor complex suggests that D-loop remodeling by this motor does not produce H-plug distortion (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), indicating that this mechanism may be selectively employed by different myosins and represents another avenue for motor specialization.
evidence: Figure 6—figure supplement 2 shows the absence of H-plug repositioning in myosin IIC.

claim: The proposed actin strain mechanism is consistent with previous functional data suggesting differential F-actin conformational dynamics in the presence of myosin V and muscle myosin S1.
source: This model is consistent with previous functional data suggesting differential F-actin conformational dynamics in the presence of myosin V and muscle myosin S1 (Prochniewicz et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Prochniewicz et al., 2010.

claim: Actin nucleotide state influences myosin VI processivity and could exert its effects via modulation of actin conformation.
source: Actin nucleotide state, a marker of filament age within the cell, influences myosin VI processivity (Zimmermann et al., 2015), and could exert its effects via such a mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zimmermann et al., 2015.

claim: Conformational changes generated at a single actomyosin VI interface could be allosterically communicated along a filament to influence the binding interactions or activity of other actin binding partners at distal sites.
source: Finally, conformational changes generated at a single actomyosin VI interface could be allosterically communicated along a filament to influence the binding interactions or activity of other actin binding partners at distal sites, consistent with previous reports of myosin VI influencing the structural dynamics and mechanical rigidity of actin (Prochniewicz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Prochniewicz et al., 2011.

claim: Myosin VI operates as either a processive dimeric transporter or as a monomeric tether.
source: In contrast to 'rower' myosins (Leibler and Huse, 1993) that generate bulk contractile forces along actin filaments through assembly into filaments, myosin VI operates as either a processive dimeric transporter (Dunn et al., 2010; Sweeney et al., 2007) or as a monomeric tether (Lister et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Defects in myosin genes have been linked to muscular dystrophies, cardiac disease, cancer, and deafness.
source: Defects in myosin genes have been linked to muscular dystrophies, cardiac disease, cancer, and deafness, highlighting the critical role of myosins in cell function and human health (Hirokawa and Takemura, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hirokawa and Takemura, 2003.

claim: The myosin superfamily features over 20 classes.
source: However, as the myosin superfamily features over 20 classes, a detailed understanding of each motor and its specific mechanisms remains incomplete (Sellers, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sellers, 2000.

claim: The enzymatic mechanism of ATP-dependent force generation on filamentous actin (F-actin) is fundamentally conserved across the myosin superfamily.
source: Despite this diversity, the enzymatic mechanism of ATP-dependent force generation on filamentous actin (F-actin) is fundamentally conserved (Figure 1A) (Geeves, 2016; Holmes, 1997; Lymn and Taylor, 1971; Sweeney and Houdusse, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and Figure 1A shows the conserved mechanochemical cycle.

claim: The motor domain (MD) binds and hydrolyzes ATP, which allosterically produces conformational changes enabling low-affinity engagement with F-actin in the pre-power stroke state.
source: The motor domain (MD) binds and hydrolyzes ATP, which allosterically produces conformational changes enabling low-affinity engagement with F-actin (Figure 1A, Pre-power stroke state).
evidence: Figure 1A shows the pre-power stroke state in the mechanochemical cycle.

claim: The transient opening of the small switch II loop (swII) adjacent to the nucleotide binding cleft allows phosphate to escape.
source: The transient opening of the small switch II loop (swII) adjacent to the nucleotide binding cleft allows phosphate to escape (Figure 1A, Pi release state)
evidence: Figure 1A shows the Pi release state.

claim: Phosphate escape triggers the transition to a moderate F-actin binding affinity ADP state accompanied by large-scale rearrangements in the converter region which are propagated through the lever arm to generate the power stroke.
source: triggering the transition to a moderate F-actin binding affinity ADP state (Figure 1A, ADP state) accompanied by large-scale rearrangements in the converter region which are propagated through the lever arm to generate the power stroke (Llinas et al., 2015).
evidence: Figure 1A shows the ADP state, and the claim is supported by citation to Llinas et al., 2015.

claim: Subsequent ADP release results in the highest affinity actin-myosin interaction (rigor state).
source: Subsequent ADP release results in the highest affinity actin-myosin interaction (Figure 1A, rigor state).
evidence: Figure 1A shows the rigor state.

claim: Re-binding of ATP into the nucleotide cleft promotes myosin dissociation from the filament and primes the motor for a successive cycle.
source: Re-binding of ATP into the nucleotide cleft then promotes myosin dissociation from the filament (Figure 1A, post-rigor state) and primes the motor for a successive cycle.
evidence: Figure 1A shows the post-rigor state.

claim: Sequence divergence of the MD across the superfamily has modulated the kinetics of the various steps of the mechanochemical cycle to tune biophysical parameters including duty cycle, ATPase rate, and force sensitivity.
source: Sequence divergence of the MD across the superfamily has modulated the kinetics of the various steps of this cycle to tune biophysical parameters including duty cycle, ATPase rate, and force sensitivity, and enabled regulation by post-translational modifications (Uyeda et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Uyeda et al., 1994.

claim: Significant sequence diversity is found on the surface of the MD which contacts F-actin, suggesting that modulation of this interface may enable optimization of motor properties for different cellular roles.
source: Significant sequence diversity is found on the surface of the MD which contacts F-actin, suggesting that modulation of this interface may enable optimization of these parameters for different cellular roles (Berg et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Berg et al., 2001.

claim: A hybrid procedure for image analysis and 3D reconstruction was developed consisting of initial alignment using an adapted EMAN2/SPARX protocol for IHRSR, followed by polishing refinement and reconstruction using FREALIGN.
source: For image analysis and 3D reconstruction, we developed a hybrid procedure consisting of initial alignment using an adapted EMAN2/SPARX (Hohn et al., 2007; Tang et al., 2007) protocol for IHRSR (Egelman, 2007), which implements refinement and reconstruction of independent half-datasets to minimize noise bias in resolution estimation and alignment, followed by polishing refinement and reconstruction of the full dataset using FREALIGN (Lyumkis et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the computational methods used, supported by citations.

claim: The MDFF approach was adapted to generate a continuous atomistic model which captures high-resolution features in the best-resolved regions of the map while avoiding over-interpretation of lower-resolution areas.
source: We therefore adapted the molecular dynamics flexible fitting (MDFF) (Trabuco et al., 2008) approach to generate a continuous atomistic model which captures high-resolution features in the best-resolved regions of the map by enabling fitting of large side-chains (Figure 1C, blue) while avoiding over-interpretation of lower-resolution areas, where the influence of the map was restricted to backbone conformation (Figure 1C, green, see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: Figure 1C shows the different treatment of regions during MDFF, and the claim is supported by citation to Trabuco et al., 2008.

claim: Mechanically gated acceleration of ADP binding has been reported to enable the motor to switch between anchor and transport functions.
source: Mechanically gated acceleration of ADP binding has been reported to enable the motor to switch between anchor and transport functions (Altman et al., 2004; Chuan et al., 2011; Robblee et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Force-dependent inhibition of ADP release has been reported based on single-molecule measurements of monomers.
source: and force-dependent inhibition of ADP release has also been reported based on single-molecule measurements of monomers (Oguchi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oguchi et al., 2008.

claim: Kinetic measurements of dimers have favored an alternative ATP-gating model over ADP release gating for coordinating heads during processive walking.
source: Gating of ADP release has been considered as a mechanism for coordinating heads during processive walking (Dunn et al., 2010; Elting et al., 2011; Oguchi et al., 2008), although kinetic measurements of dimers have favored an alternative ATP-gating model (Sweeney et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Pioneering low-resolution cryo-EM studies suggested that a minor repositioning of the lever arm accompanies the transition from ADP to rigor.
source: Pioneering low-resolution cryo-EM studies suggested that a minor repositioning of the lever arm accompanies the transition from ADP to rigor (Wells et al., 1999)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wells et al., 1999.

claim: Myosin-generated forces have been implicated in influencing actin conformation.
source: In addition to regulating the mechanochemical cycle, myosin-generated forces have been implicated in influencing actin conformation (Anson et al., 1995; Orlova and Egelman, 1997; Prochniewicz et al., 2010; Prochniewicz and Thomas, 2001)
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Myosin II filaments induce severing events in F-actin.
source: Myosin II filaments induce severing events in F-actin (Vogel et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vogel et al., 2013.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of rigor myosin IIC bound to actin reveals subtle actin conformational changes in response to myosin binding.
source: and the cryo-EM structure of rigor myosin IIC bound to actin reveals subtle actin conformational changes in response to myosin binding (von der Ecken et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to von der Ecken et al., 2016.

claim: Moderate-resolution cryo-EM reconstructions of myosin V bound to F-actin suggest that binding by this motor may induce changes in actin twist, without further modulation of actin conformation during the mechanochemical cycle.
source: Moderate-resolution cryo-EM reconstructions of myosin V bound to F-actin in nucleotide-free and ADP states suggest that binding by this motor may induce changes in actin twist, without further modulation of actin conformation during the mechanochemical cycle; however, the level of detail in the maps presented in this study precluded a detailed description of actin conformational changes (Wulf et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wulf et al., 2016.

claim: Actin structural rearrangements were proposed to play a role in myosin VI motor activity and step size based on early single-molecule tracking and negative-stain electron microscopy studies.
source: Actin structural rearrangements, such as altered helical twist, were also proposed to play a role in myosin VI motor activity and step size on the basis of early single-molecule tracking and negative-stain electron microscopy studies (Nishikawa et al., 2002) that predated our current structural understanding of the myosin VI dimer (Houdusse and Sweeney, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nishikawa et al., 2002 and Houdusse and Sweeney, 2016.
